question: on winter days, does the Ti flange with its capsule make the cambium under the Ø15–Ø29.8 ring colder than under bark without it, and how does the answer move with the sky and the sun?
method: 1D implicit column on 78's grid (properties of 58) with a surface energy balance — convection, long-wave exchange with a clear (Brutsaert 1975) or overcast sky and air-temperature surroundings at sky view 0.5, and optionally ERA5 diffuse sun — over 30 ERA5 years; under the flange the balance acts through a fin of A_fin/A_contact

brutsaert.coefficient_read_via: Crawford & Duchon 1999, J. Appl. Meteor. 38:474 (open text)

forms.linear: ours — the two sky ends mixed by the cover
forms.b82: Brutsaert 1982 as printed in Herrero & Polo 2012 eq. 8, C = 0.22

beam_sun.method: ERA5 DNI on a vertical trunk face at each azimuth (outward normal, clockwise from north) through the sun's position by NOAA GML's General Solar Position Calculations, averaged over the hour each radiation value averages; the stem shades the face when the sun is behind it; open field — no crown, neighbour trunk or horizon; with each real-cloud form and its diffuse; the records here carry no ground-reflected light, its two ends are in `ground_reflected`

ground_reflected.method: isotropic ground reflection on a vertical face, ρ·GHI through the ground's view share (1 − F) with each column's own absorptance; ρ switched by a reanalysis's snow depth; open field (GHI = ERA5 DNI on the horizontal plus ERA5 diffuse), so it rides with the beam only

albedo_sources.snow: Baker, Ruschy & Wall 1990, J. Appl. Meteor. 29:179, doi:10.1175/1520-0450(1990)029<0179:TADOPS>2.0.CO;2 — ≈ 0.80 the mean the day after a snowfall; 0.50 the cutoff their deep-snow (≥ 10.2 cm) decay sample is selected by — not a measured albedo
albedo_sources.ground: Baker & Ruschy 1988, J. Appl. Meteor. 27:244, doi:10.1175/1520-0450(1988)027<0244:HAVASP>2.0.CO;2, Table 2 medians — April 0.18, October 0.24

beam_sun.deharden_reading: Sakai 1968, Contr. Inst. Low Temp. Sci. B15:1, via canon 01_04 §3.1 — exposure above it is the CAUSE of winter dehardening; hours above it are counted, never priced as a dose

verdict.text: The sign of the shift depends on the sky and the sun. Clear sky, no sun — the end most favourable to the flange: the tied median is -2.6…-0.5 K (warmer under the flange), because a long-wave deficit depresses flat bark (-6.9 K at its equilibrium) more than the capsule (-5.7 K) — with the capsule's h_c set to bark's the tied median turns +0.4 K. Overcast, no sun: +0.3…+0.6 K (colder) — the fin's conductance to the air (6× bark's) makes the ring follow the air's daily fall. Diffuse sun on both raises it again (bark banks the gain, the fin sheds it): clear -1.7…+0.1 K, overcast +1.1…+1.4 K. The worst day of the four ends is +4.6 K colder (overcast_diffuse_sun, tied). Decoupled — the flange's band alone, 0.54× the ring — moves the same way with smaller medians. Weighed by the site's real cloud (ERA5: winter median cover 0.98, above 0.8 in 72% of winter hours), the answer turns on how cover becomes sky radiation, and the one measurement in hand (a mountain station, by day) does not settle it for a valley cell at night: if full cover radiates as a black body at air temperature (the two ends mixed by the cover), the tied flange is colder on 26%–68% of frost days without sun and 69%–89% with diffuse sun (median +0.5…+1.2 K); with Brutsaert 1982's factor at its original C 0.22, which leaves a fully covered winter sky short of a black body, on 0%–37% and 11%–76%. On the cold days (bark below -10 °C), the tail an injury threshold sits in: 58%–88% colder under the first, 0%–48% under the second without sun. Beam sun on the trunk face — swept over its azimuth with open-field ERA5 DNI, the upper end of beam — moves the shift against the diffuse-only weighing (the median by -0.01…+2.05 K): tied -0.8…+1.2 K on a north face, +0.8…+3.0 K on a south one, colder there on 73%–100% of frost days — the bark banks the beam the fin sheds. In absolute terms the beam still warms the spot: its coldest hour is warmer on a south face than on a north one in every cell (tied +0.3…+1.7 K). The same beam lifts the cambium above ≈ 13 °C, the exposure Sakai names as what dehardens, under bark more often than under the flange in every winter total (not in every month: in month(s) [11] of faces [0, 45, 315] the flange has a few more): on a south face 293–474 hours a winter without it against 22–103 under the tied flange (north 6–28 against 5–21). So this axis does not choose an azimuth by itself: the absolute frost floor under the flange favours the south, its hours of dehardening the north, and only a measure of how much the node perturbs the cambium points one way; weighing them needs a dose-response no primary gives. Ground-reflected light, open field like the beam and on every face — snow on the ground from a reanalysis checked against a station (two checked; the low end takes the one with less winter snow where snow masks the ground, era5_land at ≥ 11 cm, with 0.5 over snow — the cutoff of Baker's deep-snow sample, not a measured albedo — and 0.18 over bare ground; the high end the one with more, era5_land at ≥ 1 cm, with 0.8 — Baker's mean the day after a snowfall — and 0.24) — adds 0.43–1.04× the model's diffuse term over the winter and moves the median shift by +0.04…+0.77 K and the coldest hour under the flange by +0.09…+1.22 K across both ends; on a south face the hours above 13 °C a winter become 349–633 under bark and 28–178 under the tied flange (north 13–133 and 7–53), and at the low end the hours above 13 °C under the tied flange no longer separate north (7–33 a winter) from south (28–134); at the high end the hours above 13 °C under the tied flange no longer separate north (8–53 a winter) from south (35–178). Read cell by cell instead — the pairing the floor reading already had, added after the data broke the declared range reading — the south has at least 2.94× the north's hours under the tied flange at either end; without reflected light the declared reading held by 0.6 h a winter. The ground's long-wave stays at air temperature under snow, and the open field is applied to every face (a stand edge facing the sun gives its north face less). The real coupling is not in the tree; 1D inflates the shift in both signs. The regional injury threshold and its corrections live in canon (docs/01_04 §3.1): it sits NEAR this model's floor, not far below it.

ceilings: beam sun is swept over the face's azimuth with open-field DNI — the upper end of BEAM (no crown, neighbour trunk or horizon; the mounting azimuth is a decision, 00_07 HW.6); ground-reflected light rides with the beam only, at two ends whose snow comes from reanalyses other than ERA5 (on our channel ERA5 carries no snow depth) checked against a station ~100 km away, and whose albedo was measured at St. Paul, Minnesota over an open agricultural plot — not under a crown, on a forest floor or at the site; the ground in the long-wave view stays at air temperature under snow too (a clear-night snow surface below the air — an extra loss — is not carried, so the floor's gain is the reflected term alone), and the open field is applied to every face (at a stand edge facing the sun the north face looks into the stand); the diffuse-only weighing carries none, so it stays the closed-stand lower end; frost days are defined by the bark of the same face, so nights the spot freezes and the sunlit bark does not are left out; real cloud (ERA5) is weighed, through two long-wave forms that disagree under full cover — which one holds at the site decides the sign, and neither form's primary was read
1D and zero contact resistance inflate the shift in both signs; the tied end is the upper end of the coupling axis only, and the two coupling ends bracket the median, not the tail
the radome↔flange coupling is not measured — decoupled and tied are its two ends
F 0.5, ε 0.90, α_bark 0.80 and the trunk's convection correlation are ours; α_fin is the radome's specified ceiling and a lighter finish enlarges the shift
no injury verdict — no frost-hardiness threshold for pine cambium in the tree
absolute minima are the model's lower bound (weeks of sunless clear sky), not a forecast
snow or rime on the bark or the radome is not modelled
the lump here is fed by the bark — it is not the capsule temperature 71 gives the EDLC floor
